Name: Talisman's South Park ontology explainer
Description: Jessica Talisman's South Park Ontology Explainer, as a rulebook: the page's ten facts, five rule switches, property wiring, provenance wording and current-value policy are rows, and every conclusion is a formula. The rules apply in three fixed strata (inverse and symmetric, then the property chain, then domain and range); property wiring that feeds an earlier stratum would need repeated rounds.

data.StringValue: Talisman's South Park ontology explainer, with a rulebook underneath

The model follows the explainer page's own script as read on 2026-11-26: its ten facts, five rules, property wiring, provenance wording and the one-current-grade-and-role policy. Her starting state is the seed: facts on, rules off.
Character and location portraits are Fandom images, linked from each Things row; South Park is the work of Trey Parker and Matt Stone.

data.Text: South Park Ontology Explainer, on one rulebook
A rulebook rebuild of the explainer by
South Park facts form a knowledge graph

An ontology defines kinds of things, their properties and rules. This knowledge graph uses those definitions to connect facts about South Park. Stan’s school facts can change while Stan stays the same person.

This version runs no reasoner in the browser. Every fact, rule switch and conclusion on the page is a row or a formula in one rulebook, compiled to Postgres views; the same rulebook also builds TypeScript, Python, an Excel workbook, OWL and documentation in 16 languages.
Drag a circle to move it. Tap a circle or a line to read its facts and sources.
Character portraits and South Park Elementary are Fandom images, linked from the rulebook’s Things table. Dashed circles mark classes; solid circles show individual things or values.

Each statement has three parts, called a triple. The subject identifies what we describe. The predicate tells how it is connected to the object. The object is the related thing or value. Select a fact to show it.
Stan can change while his identity stays the same

The grade-5 and leaving-school buttons imagine future changes so you can see how the model responds. They do not report events from the show. Stan is allowed to graduate. The database does not get a vote.
Rules add facts to the graph

An inference is a new conclusion from facts and a rule. Reasoning means following rules step by step to reach or check conclusions. Here the rulebook does that work: each rule is a switch, and every conclusion is a formula.
Try Sharon, is parent of, Stan. Then try Sharon, is parent of, Randy with the disjoint rule on.

For has grade level, enter an integer (a number with no fractional part), such as 4 or 5. This form checks integer input as an application check. For has role, enter text such as Student. A new grade or role replaces that person’s previous active value in this page’s current record. Uncheck a role fact to clear it.
Enter an integer (a number with no fractional part) for {field}. This is an application input check.
{subject} now has {kind} {value} in this page’s current record. The person’s identifier stays the same.
“{fact}” is not in this rulebook yet. Every fact the page can hold is a row; a new name or value needs new rows.
Stan is explicitly recorded as a Person.
Stan’s explicit Person statement is not selected.
Hover a dotted value to read its rule and the facts it came from. Every rule on this page is in the rulebook below, and every projection of it agrees.
Explainer: every rule, down to the stated facts
Excel workbook with every rule as a live formula
Fandom supplies the character and location images

A rebuild of Jessica Talisman’s South Park Ontology Explainer for Intentional Arrangement, made from a rulebook. The model, wording and layout follow her page. South Park is the work of Trey Parker and Matt Stone; the portraits are Fandom images.
